title: Why Would Anyone Support an Evil Empire?

voice.direction: A calm, curious guide, never sarcastic about the empire's people. A real question on the hook; plain and practical on 'Ask the people holding it up'. Each supporter is said with sympathy, a short beat before each reason. 'Complainers get a knock at night' is quiet, not dramatic. 'And nobody can picture anything better' lands softly. The lesson is clear and sure; the share CTA friendly. No trailer voice.

lines.text: If your empire is so evil, why hasn't everyone rebelled?
Ask the people holding it up.
The farmer gets safe roads, and bread every winter.
The clerk remembers the chaos before the throne.
The soldier's mother needs his wage.
The neighbour keeps quiet. Complainers get a knock at night.
And nobody can picture anything better.
A villainous empire is believable when its supporters aren't villains.
Share this with someone writing a one-dimensional villainous empire.

shots.purpose: The reveal and the lesson: the pillars were people all along, each with an understandable reason, and the fifth pillar is an absence (no better option). Then the shareable thought.
shots.visual: The pillar stack returns; each stone pillar becomes the supporter we met (BREAD, ORDER, THE WAGE, FEAR); a fifth, empty dashed pillar appears: NOTHING BETTER. The stack lifts and the lesson lands below: 'STILL CRUEL. STILL STANDING. / Its supporters aren't villains.'

shots.music: G to D major, warm; fades fully before the last frame.

lesson: An oppressive empire survives because many ordinary people hold it up, each for an understandable reason: prosperity (bread, safe roads), stability (order after remembered chaos), self-interest (the wage), fear, and the absence of any better alternative. A villainous empire is believable when its supporters are not villains.

youtube.description:
If your empire is so evil, why hasn't everyone rebelled?

Ask the people holding it up. In Valdren, the farmer gets safe roads and bread every winter. The clerk remembers the chaos before the throne. The soldier's mother needs his wage. The neighbour keeps quiet, because complainers get a knock at night. And nobody can picture anything better.

Bread, order, a wage, fear and no better option: five pillars, and not one of them is a villain. Real regimes last on mixtures of force, loyalty, stability, propaganda, prosperity and fear. Your empire can stay cruel. It becomes believable when its supporters have reasons a reader understands.
